item.title: Pakistani astronauts learn Chinese, training program offers experience for future missions: technical expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 10:01:00
This photo taken on Nov. 17, 2026 shows the combination of the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft and a Long March-2F carrier rocket being transferred to the launch area. Photo: Xinhua The Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft is scheduled for launch, as the launch site for the spaceflight mission has already completed all preparations, with equipment, personnel and systems ready. Shi Yusheng, a technical expert at the Astronaut Center of China, told the Global Times that although the Pakistani astronauts initially had a relatively limited foundation in Chinese, their language skills have improved through training and their own hard work, and are now sufficient to meet the requirements of mission execution. The two Pakistani astronauts have been very diligent, studying Chinese every day. Toward the later stages of their training, they were even taught some classic Chinese poems, Shi added. All user interfaces on the space station are in Chinese. Targeted training and support have been provided to Pakistani astronauts regarding the relevant symbols they need to recognize, the tasks they need to perform, and the Chinese-language content involved. If astronauts from other countries enter China's space station in the future, can the training program and related materials developed for the Pakistani astronauts be reused? Shi explained that this mission is both pioneering and highly challenging. To accomplish the mission, the Center has not only conducted relevant training over the past few months but also carried out extensive preparatory work in the lead-up to the mission. The experience gained during training, as well as the training materials and handouts developed, will provide valuable insights and serve as a reference for future missions of a similar nature, Shi said.

item.title: Shenzhou-24 crew unveiled; first foreign astronaut joins China's space mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 09:51:00
China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) on November 24, 2026, unveiled the Shenzhou-24 crew: spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo (center), flight engineer Wu Yi (right), and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali (left). The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) on Tuesday unveiled the Shenzhou-24 crew: spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi, and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali. Tang will serve as the mission commander. This marks the first crew in China's manned space programs to include a foreign astronaut. Commander Tang previously flew on the Shenzhou 12 and Shenzhou 17 missions and is set to become the first Chinese astronaut to visit the Tiangong space station three times. Wu Yi is a member of the third cohort of Chinese astronauts. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is among the first foreign astronauts selected under the cooperation agreement between China and Pakistan. Both Wu Yi and Muhammad Zeeshan Ali will be making their maiden spaceflight, according to CMSA. Under the mission plan, after a short duration stay aboard the space station, the first foreign astronaut will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft. Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, will remain in orbit to take part in the Shenzhou-24 mission. He will be China's first astronaut to complete a one year in orbit stay, experiencing the full cycle of "seasons" aboard the Tiangong. The three astronauts of Shenzhou-24 will meet with Chinese and international journalists at the Wentian Pavilion of the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Gansu Province, on Tuesday.

item.title: US stocks surge as Nvidia's Huang reinstatement reignites AI trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 08:03:00
A trader works on the trading floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City, the United States, Nov. 23, 2026. U.S. stocks ended higher on Monday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,447.98 points, or 3.01 percent, to 49,595.31. The S&P 500 added 326.78 points, or 4.73 percent, to 7,237.17. The Nasdaq Composite Index increased by 1,471.83 points, or 6.51 percent, to 24,089.56. (Xinhua/Liu Yanan) US stocks surged on Monday as Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO reignited the AI trade, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite posting their biggest single-day gains since April 9, 2025. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,447.98 points, or 3.01 percent, to 49,595.31. The S&P 500 added 326.78 points, or 4.73 percent, to 7,237.17. The Nasdaq Composite Index increased by 1,471.83 points, or 6.51 percent, to 24,089.56. Nine of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended higher, with technology leading the gainers by adding 9.03 percent, while energy led the laggards by falling 1.32 percent. Oil prices fell sharply as concerns over a global supply glut outweighed risks to supplies from the Middle East. West Texas Intermediate crude for January delivery dropped 3.88 percent to settle at 80.17 U.S. dollars a barrel, its lowest level since August, while Brent crude fell 3.46 percent to 89.37 dollars a barrel. On the corporate front, Nvidia surged 31.48 percent after its board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as president and CEO, effective immediately. The chipmaker recorded the largest single-day increase in market capitalization on record, adding nearly 1 trillion dollars and bringing its valuation back close to 4 trillion dollars. Chip stocks rallied across the board, with Micron Technology jumping around 19 percent, Marvell Technology up 18.37 percent, and Intel climbing 16.34 percent. Advanced Micro Devices gained 6.85 percent, while Dell Technologies rocketed over 20 percent. CoreWeave popped 22.32 percent and Oracle jumped 12.34 percent. "The shocking decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO helps to remove a key level of uncertainty from the AI trade, which has been suffering in recent weeks," said Glen Smith, chief investment officer at GDS Wealth Management. The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street's fear gauge, fell nearly 26 percent to 26.62. The rally in chip stocks also lifted other technology shares. Tesla surged 11.46 percent, while Alphabet and Meta Platforms each jumped over 6 percent. On the economic front, S&P Global's flash Purchasing Managers' Index showed U.S. business activity growth easing to a four-month low in November. The composite index fell to 54.6 from 55.9 in October, while the services index slipped to 54.7 and the manufacturing index fell to 54.5. Investors also continued to weigh the prospect of a quarter-point interest rate hike at the Fed's December meeting, with the October personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, due for release on Wednesday. item.title: Jensen Huang's dramatic reinstatement: Will there be 'Jensen Li' or 'Jensen Zhang'?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 00:33:00
A television broadcasts Nvidia news on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in the US on November 23, 2026. An overnight bounce in stocks erupted into a surge after Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive officer recharged artificial-intelligence bets. Photo: VCG On November 23, Nvidia announced that the company's board of directors had unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang to his positions as President, CEO, and a member of the board, effective immediately. The announcement stated that the board received input from senior levels of the US government and, based on that input, determined that Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk. Thus, this farce - first instigated by US media and rife with gossip, conspiracy theories, and Hollywood-style drama - has taken yet another dramatic turn. The statement that "Jensen Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk" is clearly a conclusion regarding the earlier allegations that he had been "infiltrated by Chinese spies." As two of the most active media players shaping the narrative around this episode, the Wall Street Journal ran a muted report after Huang's reinstatement, while the New York Times framed his comeback as entirely down to "Trump's backing." Both outlets must be displeased with how things turned out. Ever since the Jensen Huang farce broke, the US public discourse has been rife with sensationalism. The behavior of certain politicians and media outlets has less to do with genuine "concern" for Jensen Huang's personal affairs or Nvidia's corporate governance than with wildcats that have caught the scent of blood and are eager to pounce. By exploiting the situation to cast aspersions on "Chinese infiltration," they have had a negative impact on American society's perception of China. It is foreseeable that the malicious attempts to sow discord in China-US relations will not automatically disappear simply because Huang has been reinstated. Their greed and prejudice remain lurking beneath the surface of American politics and public discourse, ready to resurface at any moment in the next "Jensen Li" or "Jensen Zhang" incident. The next round of "witch hunts" may not appear in the form of "spies," but it could lurk in various hidden corners: investigation letters, delays in export licenses, congressional hearings, and baseless "exposés" in the media... They do not need to be ultimately confirmed; they only need to create enough uncertainty at critical junctures to make companies self-censor and self-restrict when making decisions. This uncertainty is, in itself, a double-edged sword that can harm both others and oneself. The dramatic turn in Jensen Huang's fate is a matter for the US itself. However, when a messy farce can quickly be linked to the "China threat," the warning is already strong enough. It reminds us that the specter of profiting from anti-China narratives still wanders through American society. We must remain vigilant.

item.title: With its own climate governance arrears unpaid, how can Western media expect China to 'pick up the tab'?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 22:52:00
COP31 President Murat Kurum (center) leaves a closing plenary session at the COP31 UN Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on November 22, 2026. The 31st COP31 failed to reach a consensus on the Antalya Pact. Photo: VCG When negotiations break down, China is blamed for being "unwilling to take the lead"; yet when China provides green production capacity to the world, some media outlets sensationalize the "China shock" and "overcapacity" narratives. Either way, China is always made to take the blame. If the West truly welcomes greater contributions from China to global emissions reduction, it should first work to remove the various discriminatory policies targeting China's new energy exports. The repeatedly extended United Nations (UN) Climate Change Conference (COP31), in Antalya, Turkey, ended in a breakdown of negotiations. This marks the first time since 2009 that a UN climate conference has "ended without agreement," and it was also the longest-running session since the first conference in 1995. Before the conference closed, Reuters, citing the US government's absence, questioned why China was unwilling to be the world's next climate leader. In this framing, obligations developed countries should honor are twisted as something they can sit back and wait for China to "pick up the tab" - an absurd inversion of accountability. The primary reason for the breakdown in negotiations at this conference was that the final draft failed to include clear provisions regarding the transition away from fossil fuels. Parties such as the European Union (EU) refused to accept the text because the final draft made no mention of fossil fuels. With nearly 200 parties harboring divergent priorities, reaching a consensus inherently requires all sides to make compromises on specific provisions. Attributing the failure of the negotiations to China's "unwillingness to take the lead" not only overlooks the concessions China made to seek consensus but also fails to explain the differences among parties regarding the transition away from fossil fuels. Not to mention that developed countries represented by Europe have come under heavy criticism during the negotiations for obstructing progress on multiple fronts, including adaptation finance and just transition. The EU's climate chief even publicly stated before the meeting that talks on "new climate finance commitments" were "dead in the water," ruling out any new commitments to large-scale climate pledges. This stance sparked dissatisfaction among many countries. Some European media outlets chose to overlook this. Instead, by citing the so-called "reluctance of China to take the lead," they sought to discredit China's efforts in addressing climate change. One cannot help but wonder whether this move is intended to evade their own historical responsibilities. Reaching a consensus requires the joint efforts of all nations, and there has long been a clear division of responsibilities regarding taking the lead in emissions reductions and providing funding. The Paris Agreement reaffirmed the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, clearly stipulating that developed countries should continue to take the lead in reducing emissions and have an obligation to provide financial assistance for mitigation and adaptation measures in developing countries. Insufficient funding will delay climate adaptation projects - such as flood control and water supply - and weaken developing countries' ability to withstand climate disasters. Leveling such accusations against China does not absolve developed countries of their financial obligations. For a transition affordable to all nations, adequate financial support must be in place, and emission reduction technologies must also be accessible at manageable costs. China's push in Antalya to discuss trade barriers was aimed precisely at this latter point. Ahead of the conference, the EU urged major emitters, including China, to step up their emission reductions, yet electric vehicles (EVs) originating in China still face additional anti-subsidy duties when entering the EU market. This contradictory approach is also reflected in the biases of Western narratives. When negotiations break down, China is blamed for being "unwilling to take the lead"; yet when China provides green production capacity to the world, the media sensationalizes the "China shock" and "overcapacity." Either way, China is always made to take the blame. If the West truly welcomes greater contributions from China to global emissions reduction, it should first work to remove the various discriminatory policies targeting China's new energy exports. According to estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA), even when emissions from both vehicle manufacturing and use are taken into account, a medium-sized battery-electric vehicle still produces fewer emissions on average than a comparable gasoline-powered vehicle. The same applies to solar photovoltaics. As solar panels become cheaper, projects previously shelved due to high costs become economically viable, allowing local communities to replace coal- or gas-fired power with solar energy sooner. The emissions reductions occur in the countries where these products are used, and helping accelerate that transition is precisely China's contribution. Imposing tariffs on Chinese products that could help reduce domestic emissions, while simultaneously urging China to do more to combat climate change, will only make it harder for those countries to achieve their own emissions reduction targets. China's enormous contributions to global climate governance in recent years are evident to all. According to IEA estimates that account for emissions from electricity generation and fuel supply, the stock of EVs was responsible for avoiding net emissions of 190 Mt CO2‑equivalent (CO2-eq) in 2025 compared with equivalent gasoline-powered vehicles, with more than half of those reductions attributable to EV deployment in China. Last year, China provided developing countries with $132 billion in clean technologies and investment, nearly matching the total climate finance provided by all developed nations in 2024. According to estimates by overseas research institutions, this year alone, China's exports of clean energy equipment are expected to reduce emissions overseas by approximately 450 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. These achievements are "unparalleled globally." During this year's climate conference, the Chinese delegation participated in negotiations and consultations on 165 agenda items and held more than 50 bilateral meetings at the ministerial level, making tremendous efforts to encourage all parties to work toward common ground. Ahead of the next round of negotiations, developed countries should translate their financial commitments into funding for concrete projects, continue to take the lead in reducing emissions at home, and give green products a fair opportunity to compete. China has already transformed many once-expensive low-carbon technologies into affordable products accessible to more countries and households, and has demonstrated that a development pathway combining wind and solar power, energy storage, and EVs is both technically and economically viable, representing one of its greatest contributions to the global low-carbon transition. It is abundantly clear that addressing climate change requires a collective effort by countries around the world.

item.title: GT Voice: South Korea's vehicle sector can steer clear of China deficit debate
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 22:37:00
An NEV manufacturing line in Southwest China's Chongqing Municipality Photo: VCG South Korea's vehicle trade deficit with China reached a record $4.231 billion in the first 10 months of this year, 4.5 times the full-year figure for 2023, according to The Chosun Daily. China's growing competitiveness in auto manufacturing is increasingly being felt in the South Korean market, but that does not mean that the two countries' economic interests are necessarily at odds. However, a more defensive view has emerged in South Korea. The Chosun Daily reported growing concerns that Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) could account for more than 50 percent of sales in South Korea next year, prompting the automotive industry to "urgently demand countermeasures." Yet there is more to this issue than competition alone. A different picture emerges from a business event in Changchun, Northeast China's Jilin Province in May. The Seoul Economic Daily reported that the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency organized an export consultation as part of stepped-up efforts to help South Korean auto parts makers tap opportunities in China, where sales of eco-friendly vehicles are growing. China is an important export market for South Korean auto parts. Although China's domestic supply chain is well established, the South Korean industry sees scope to expand exports in specialized fields such as automotive electronics, software and lightweight materials. This points to another dimension of the trade that bilateral statistics rarely capture. South Korean-made components can enter China's automotive supply chains, become part of vehicles assembled by Chinese manufacturers and serve consumers in China and overseas. Some of those vehicles may even be exported back to South Korea. In trade statistics, the components are recorded as South Korean exports to China, while the finished vehicles are counted as Chinese exports to South Korea, adding to South Korea's recorded automotive trade deficit with China. Seen in this light, making the trade deficit the focus of the debate misses the point. The vehicle industries of the two neighboring countries are already intertwined through complementary strengths. As supply chains grow more complex, the distinction between trade surpluses and deficits becomes less meaningful, with companies on both sides contributing to production and benefiting from one another's markets. What South Korea's auto industry urgently needs is not a response to its trade deficit with China, let alone a demand for countermeasures. It is to strengthen its own competitiveness, move up the value chain and find new sources of growth. Put simply, the industry should be moving forward, not stopping to defend itself against China. South Korea is no newcomer to the global vehicle industry. It has established internationally recognized brands and a substantial manufacturing base. The industry put in a strong performance in October, after a period of month-to-month fluctuations. Its automobile exports rose 18.1 percent year-on-year to $6.55 billion in October, while domestic production increased 25.8 percent to 381,000 units. Vehicles are among South Korea's most important export products. The country's auto industry has long been closely connected to international markets, with overseas sales playing an important part in its development. Its next phase of growth will depend on strengthening its position in established markets while making further inroads into emerging ones. Expanding its global reach will be essential to sustaining the industry's growth. Competition between the Chinese and South Korean auto industries is real, but it is only part of the picture. There is also scope for cooperation, particularly across the parts supply chain. Such cooperation can benefit both sides, helping South Korean suppliers strengthen their competitiveness and reach customers in third-party markets. As the global auto industry moves toward electrification, the opportunities extend well beyond the two countries' bilateral trade. Emerging markets in particular offer considerable room for growth as more countries embark on the transition to electric mobility. South Korea's auto industry has little to gain from being caught up in debates over whether its trade with China is in surplus or deficit. What matters more is making better use of cooperation in regional supply chains to strengthen its own capabilities, further expand its presence in international markets and help drive the transition to electric mobility in emerging economies.

item.title: From novelty to trend: How smart wearables are opening a fresh consumer frontier
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 21:43:00
Buyers try on smart glasses at the service robotics exhibition area of the 140th China Import and Export Fair (Canton Fair) in Guangzhou, South China's Guangdong Province, on October 17, 2026. Photo: VCG Every morning, when a resident of Beijing's Dongcheng district surnamed Zhou lifts her wrist, her smartwatch reads her heart rate, blood oxygen, pulse, and sleep patterns, and a one-page health report arrives on her phone. The daily "micro-checkup" has become routine in her household. Not far away, another local resident, surnamed Li, snaps photos with a pair of artificial intelligence (AI) glasses in the street. "AI glasses are really convenient, especially when I'm out travelling. I can take photos and shoot videos whenever I want, and they transfer straight to my phone, so it's easy to share them on WeChat Moments or edit them into a video," Li told the Global Times. The two scenes sit at the opposite ends of a shift underway in China's consumer electronics market. The wearables, once synonymous with the watches and the fitness bands, now extend across the body - AI glasses, smart rings, bone-conduction earphones, powered exoskeletons - with use cases spreading from sleep tracking and business communication to rehabilitation. The numbers have followed. In September, KPMG released a report on China's smart wearables market, highlighting that China's smart wearables market grew from 69.5 billion yuan ($9.8 billion) in 2021 to 105.3 billion yuan in 2025, a compound annual growth rate of 11 percent. That pace is close to the 12.2 percent recorded globally over the same period. Category data points to where the new demand is concentrated. In the first three quarters of 2026, sales revenue from smart glasses on major e-commerce platforms rose 110 percent, while revenue from exoskeleton walking aid devices increased 46.4 percent and that from embodied intelligent robots rose 22.6 percent, according to data from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce. Residents' consumption is continuing to upgrade toward development-oriented, quality-driven spending, with demand steadily rising for fitness, health management and emotional companionship. New scenarios built around wearable devices are emerging rapidly, giving rise to a smart wearables market that is richly layered and finely segmented by use case, Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Monday. Powering up with AI Product-side innovation has been a key engine driving smart wearables out of their niche, but it is not the only one. On April 27, at the China (Anhui) Science and Technology Innovation Achievement Transformation Fair, a teenager, who otherwise cannot stand on his own, tried out a lower-limb rehabilitation exoskeleton robot equipped with a brain-computer interface (BCI) developed by Aibo Intelligent Technology, iFlytek's assistive technology subsidiary. Using the device's high-performance actuators and a hybrid force-position control algorithm, the user was able to move forward as the robotic legs guided his gait. The iFlytek Aibo HM-700 series of exoskeleton robots integrates an intelligent power system, advanced sensor technology, and smart control algorithms to detect a wearer's movement intentions in real time, providing precise, efficient assistance for hip flexion, according to the information the company shared with the Global Times on Monday. By offering powered support for activities such as walking or navigating stairs, the system alleviates the burden on the lower limbs and reduces physical exertion. The company said the lower-limb exoskeleton robots are currently in use across more than 100 hospitals nationwide, having served patients on more than 10,000 occasions. Targeting market demand, more scenario innovation is taking root on the supply side. Alibaba is accelerating its wearable AI strategy with the global debut of Qwen Glasses at Mobile World Congress Barcelona, unifying its AI ecosystem under the flagship Qwen brand, Alibaba said in March 2026. The latest Qwen Glasses run on Alibaba's most advanced Qwen AI model, enabling real-time translation, high-definition (HD) capture, meeting transcription, and visual recognition. The company said in March that Qwen Glasses would fully integrate with the Qwen App. Users in China would soon be able to complete hands-free actions, such as ordering food delivery, booking hotels or hailing rides, via simple voice commands, the company said. As AI wearables have upgraded their "perception," Chinese companies, with stronger manufacturing integration and faster market iteration in smart home, electric mobility and consumer robotics, are better able to "proactively understand user intent" through multi-sensor fusion and compact versions of large language models (LLMs) running on-device, Tian Feng, former dean of SenseTime's Intelligence Industry Research Institute, told the Global Times on Monday. In an interview with the Global Times, Gian Paolo Bassi, Senior Vice President of Mainstream Innovation and Customer Role Experience at France-based Dassault Systèmes, said that China is one of the world's most important and dynamic AI markets, with its own LLMs and a wide range of other AI tools. The company regards China as an ideal testing ground for deploying and iterating industrial AI, because its computing capacity ranks among the largest anywhere, and it offers every kind of LLM and AI tool, Bassi noted. Backed by the industry chain Beyond the products themselves, it is a mature, densely packed industrial base that gives China's smart wearables industry its ability to answer fragmented demand fast. In Huaqiangbei, the Shenzhen district known as "China's No.1 electronics street," more than 115,000 businesses supply the world with over 1 million types of electronic components and consumer devices. Because the full chain - from design and engineering to tooling, assembly, marketing and export - sits inside that footprint, the district has compressed the product cycle to what local officials describe as "designed today, mass-produced tomorrow, shipped overseas within a week," the Xinhua News Agency reported on Sunday. "Smart wearables sit at the intersection of technology-intensive and manufacturing-intensive work, and their competitiveness depends on efficient coordination between upstream and downstream players," Hu said. Regions such as the Yangtze River Delta and the Pearl River Delta have already built industrial clusters spanning chips, sensors, and finished-device assembly; the technological strength of leading firms and the flexible production capacity of specialist suppliers along the chain reinforce each other, together forming an overall competitive advantage and steadily shoring up the industry's "smart" manufacturing foundation, Hu noted. In June this year, China's Ministry of Commerce and seven other government departments released an implementation guideline document to accelerate the development of "AI plus" consumption. Regarding goods consumption, the document calls for increasing the supply of new AI products, upgrading consumer electronics, household appliances and home products, cultivating the smart wearables market, and promoting AI-powered robots for eldercare, companionship and daily assistance. The China Internet Network Information Center said in March of this year that in 2025, the number of AI enterprises in China exceeded 6,000, with the scale of the core industry projected to surpass 1.2 trillion yuan. Data released by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) showed that in 2025, China became the world's leading holder of AI patents, accounting for 60 percent of the global total. Several interviewees told the Global Times that China's smart wearables industry is now entering a stage of high-quality development. Going forward, as technology keeps advancing, sub-segments mature, and wearables become more deeply embedded in public settings, the devices will reach every corner of daily life, making them an important pillar of a new phase of consumption upgrading, they said.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun When asked whether the Chinese side considered the ICC's investigation into Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, and the subsequent issuance of arrest warrants against them over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, an abuse of judicial power, given that the heads of state of China, Russia, and the US had recently agreed that the ICC and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday that China supports all efforts on the Palestinian issue that contribute to achieving fairness and justice and upholding the authority of international law. item.title: China's flu activity reaches moderate level, with three strains circulating simultaneously: reports
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 13:30:00
Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News China's latest influenza surveillance data indicate that flu activity nationwide has reached a moderate level, with three strains circulating at the same time this season, according to media reports. Medical experts said that the flu vaccine offers protection against all three strains, underscoring the importance of boosting vaccination rates and raising public awareness of the vaccine. Northern China has seen a sharp rise in flu positivity rates, while southern regions remain at fluctuating levels of activity, with clustered outbreaks increasing from the previous period, according to data released by the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, CCTV News reported. A notable feature of this year's flu season is the simultaneous circulation of three influenza strains - A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and B(Victoria) - with their respective proportions continuing to shift, the report said. In October, A(H3N2) was overwhelmingly dominant. By November, however, the proportion of A(H1N1) had risen steadily, making it the predominant strain, while A(H3N2) had fallen to below 20 percent. B(Victoria), meanwhile, has maintained a relatively stable share and continued to circulate. The coexistence of multiple influenza strains and the rapid shift in the predominant strain are the most notable features of this year's flu season, posing new challenges for prevention, CCTV said. The risk of being infected by different flu strains in succession has increased, as cross-protection among influenza strains is relatively weak, said Li Tongzeng, a chief physician with the respiratory and infectious diseases department at Beijing You'an Hospital. "For example, contracting influenza A does not rule out a subsequent influenza B infection, while infection with A(H3N2) offers limited protection against A(H1N1), leaving people susceptible to reinfection with a different strain," he added, according to the CCTV report. Li recommended vaccination, noting that the trivalent influenza vaccine offers protection against all three circulating viruses. For the general public, there is little need to focus too much on whether an infection is influenza A or B, as their clinical symptoms are similar, including fever, headache, sore throat, cough, muscle aches and pronounced fatigue, the expert noted. Influenza A and B viruses circulate every year, and existing flu vaccines provide protection against both, President of Shenzhen Third People's Hospital Lu Hongzhou told the Global Times on Monday. The priority in China, therefore, is to increase annual influenza vaccination rates and strengthen public awareness through science-based public health education. Also, existing antiviral medications are effective against both influenza A and B. The key is to obtain an early diagnosis, confirm whether the infection is influenza, and begin treatment promptly, Lu added.

item.title: HKSAR Election Committee polls highlight strengths of new electoral system, high-quality democracy: central authorities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 12:06:00
The 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections of Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) was successfully held on November 22, 2026. Photo: Screenshot from news.gov.hk The 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) were successfully held on Sunday, recording a 98.79 percent turnout, with 5,640 people voting. The election fully upheld the principle of "patriots administering Hong Kong" and highlighted the strengths of the city's new electoral system, marking another important step in advancing democracy with Hong Kong characteristics, a spokesperson for the Liaison Office of Central Government in the HKSAR said on Monday. The HKSAR Chief Executive John Lee on Sunday congratulated those elected, describing the poll as an example of healthy competition among patriots. He urged the new members to contribute to the long-term success of the "One Country, Two Systems" principle. Liang Haiming, chairman of the China Silk Road iValley Research Institute and dean of the Belt and Road Research Institute at Hainan University, told the Global Times on Monday that the new electoral system has three key strengths: establishing a common political foundation under the principle of "patriots administering Hong Kong" while safeguarding constitutional order; promoting balanced participation by accommodating the interests of different sectors; and enhancing political effectiveness by encouraging candidates to compete on the basis of their policy platforms, capabilities and performance. According to Liang, the key to developing democracy with Hong Kong characteristics lies in upholding "One Country, Two Systems," taking local circumstances into account, and improving governance effectiveness. The new electoral system aims to ensure the selection of capable leaders, address public concerns and translate institutional strengths into tangible improvements in people's livelihoods and social stability. The spokesperson of the liaison office said the elections were held at a significant time as HKSAR entered a new stage in implementing "One Country, Two Systems," rolled out its first five-year plan and prepared to mark the 30th anniversary of its return to China. The new members, whose term largely coincides with the five-year plan's implementation period, are expected to help the HKSAR government turn its development vision into reality, amid strong public attention and expectations. According to Liang, the new members can help provide policy continuity and align national development priorities with Hong Kong's strengths in finance, innovation and technology, and shipping, while addressing local needs in housing, employment and elderly care. The elections demonstrated the strengths of Hong Kong's new electoral system, including broad representation, political inclusiveness, balanced participation and fair competition. A total of 31 subsectors saw more candidates than available seats, with some recording contests of 25 candidates for 15 seats and 23 for 15, according to the spokesperson. According to the spokesperson, the diverse backgrounds of the candidates, ranging from young professionals and academics to Olympic medalists, musicians with disabilities and foreign bank executives, demonstrated balanced participation and merit-based selection. Li Xiaobing, a Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan affairs expert from Nankai University, said the figures demonstrate broader and more extensive democratic participation, with more people willing to engage in the electoral process. The members drawn from Hong Kong's political, cultural, business and professional sectors represent key forces in the city's development. As a foundational institution in association with the chief executive election and the Legislative Council's nomination and election processes, the committee's active participation reflects confidence in Hong Kong's political future and development, Li told the Global Times on Monday.
